newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's EBS calls for more land for new housing.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's EBS calls for more land for new housing.

text.p: EBS Building Society on Wednesday called on the government and local authorities to increase the amount of land available for new housing.

Chairman Henry O'Dwyer told the annual meeting that he shared the widespread concern at the rapid increase in Irish house prices which he said was primarily due to a growing mismatch between the supply of and demand for housing.
"This country has been very successful in delivering many new jobs for young people who in years past would have been forced to emigrate," O'Dwyer told members of the building society.

"Let us hope that we do not deny those young people the opportunity of owning a home of their own. Ireland is not over-populated and there is no shortage of land. We trust that the authorities will focus their attention on freeing the supply side of the equation."
Irish house prices have risen strongly over the last two years with the cost of second hand homes in the capital rising by 20 percent last year alone.
O'Dwyer said EBS had not contributed to house price inflation through excessive or imprudent lending and most EBS loans came within traditional guidelines.
Loans outside the guideline limits were only made occasionally and when it was established, following careful examination and assessment, that the borrower could afford it.
He also said the board remained committed to keeping the EBS in customer-ownership.
"As a customer-owned institution, our aim is to have the lowest possible interest margin consistent with prudent financial management," he said.
O'Dwyer said that EBS had deferred a 0.25 percentage point increase in mortgage rates implemented by other lending institutions last September.
The deferral was initially made until May 1, 1997 but in view of the fact that borrowing rates may be on the way down again, the building society plans to continue to defer the rate increase.
"We do not expect to have to adjust our rates until the next general rate adjustment," O'Dwyer said.
